passages.title: Kawah Ijen
text: Kawah Ijen is a volcano on the border of Banyuwangi and Bondowoso in East Java. It is about 2,800 metres high and is part of a group of volcanoes called the Ijen Plateau. The volcano is famous around the world for two things: a bright turquoise lake and the blue fire that appears at night.

The crater lake is about one kilometre wide. Its water looks beautiful, but it is one of the most acidic lakes on Earth, so nobody can swim in it. On windy days, clouds of yellow-white smoke rise from the edge of the lake and cover the crater walls.

The blue fire is the result of sulphuric gas. When the gas comes out of cracks in the rocks, it meets the air and burns with an electric-blue flame. The flame is only visible in the dark, so most visitors start hiking at about one o'clock in the morning. The hike from the Paltuding car park to the crater rim takes around two hours.

Kawah Ijen is also a workplace. Every day, local miners walk down into the crater and break pieces of solid sulphur. They carry the sulphur up the steep path in two baskets on a bamboo pole. Each load can weigh more than seventy kilograms.

Because of the smoke, visitors are advised to wear a gas mask, which can be rented at the car park. Warm clothes are also important, as the temperature near the top can drop below ten degrees Celsius before sunrise.

passages.title: My Grandmother's Kitchen
text: My grandmother's kitchen in Klaten is the place I miss most when I am at school in the city. It is not a big or modern kitchen. In fact, it is small, a little dark, and always smells of smoke and spices. But for me, it is the warmest room in the world.

The kitchen has a floor of red clay tiles that feel cool under my feet. Along one wall there is a long wooden table, where my grandmother prepares vegetables and grinds chilli with a stone mortar. Above the table hang woven bamboo baskets of different sizes. The largest one is for rice, and the small ones keep shallots and garlic dry.

In the corner stands an old clay stove that uses firewood. My grandmother still prefers it to the gas stove my uncle bought her. She says rice and vegetables cooked over wood taste better, and I have to agree. On the shelf next to the stove, there is a row of glass jars filled with dried anchovies, palm sugar, and homemade chilli paste.

The best part of the kitchen, however, is the small window that looks out to the rice fields. In the morning, sunlight comes through it and falls on the table, and I can hear the farmers talking as they walk to work. Whenever I sit there with a cup of sweet tea, I feel calm and happy.

passages.title: The Javan Rhinoceros
text: The Javan rhinoceros is one of the rarest large animals on Earth. Fewer than eighty of them are believed to live today, and all of them are found in only one place: Ujung Kulon National Park, at the western tip of Java.

A Javan rhino is smaller than its African cousins, but it is still a huge animal. An adult can be about three metres long and weigh up to 2,300 kilograms. Its grey skin has deep folds that make the animal look as if it is wearing armour. Unlike the Indian rhino, it has only one horn, and the horn is short, usually less than twenty-five centimetres. Female Javan rhinos often have no horn at all, only a small bump.

Javan rhinos live alone, except for mothers with their young. They spend most of the day in thick forest near rivers and mud pools. They love to roll in mud, because it protects their skin from insects and keeps them cool. They eat leaves, young shoots, and fallen fruit from more than a hundred kinds of plants.

Because the animals are shy and the forest is dense, scientists rarely see them. Instead, they study the rhinos using hidden video cameras placed along the animals' paths. The videos help the park rangers count the rhinos and check whether the young ones are healthy.

(3) Miners carry the sulphur in baskets on a bamboo pole.
questions.explanation: (1) benar sesuai paragraf 3. (2) salah: pendakian sekitar dua jam. (3) benar: two baskets on a bamboo pole.
